title: Identify and recognise factors influencing agricultural enterprise selection

lessons.title: Natural and physical factors
lessons.html:
What is an agricultural enterprise?

An enterprise is one farming activity that produces a product for sale or use, for example a beef herd, a broiler unit, a maize crop, an avocado orchard, a vegetable garden or a goat flock. Choosing the right enterprise is one of the most important decisions a farmer makes, because it ties up land, money and labour for months or years.

No enterprise suits every farm. The right choice depends on many factors. We start with the natural and physical ones, which the farmer cannot easily change.

Climate

  • Rainfall – how much, and when. Summer rainfall areas suit maize and soya; the winter rainfall Western Cape suits wheat, wine grapes and deciduous fruit.
  • Temperature and frost – bananas, mangoes and macadamias need warm, frost-free areas such as the Lowveld; apples need cold winters.
  • Hail, wind and drought risk.

Soil

  • Depth, texture (sandy, loam, clay), drainage and fertility.
  • Shallow or stony soils may suit only grazing.
  • Deep, well-drained soils suit orchards and many crops.

Water

Is water available for irrigation, and does the farm have the legal right to use it under the National Water Act 36 of 1998? Without water, only dryland crops or extensive livestock may be possible.

Land and terrain

  • Slope: steep land is at risk of erosion if ploughed and may suit only grazing or forestry.
  • Size of the farm: some enterprises need large areas, such as extensive cattle or sheep in the Karoo.
  • Veld type and carrying capacity for livestock.

Pests and diseases

Some areas have diseases that limit livestock, for example ticks and tick-borne diseases, or pests that make some crops hard to grow.

lessons.title: Economic, market and personal factors
lessons.html:
Market factors

  • Is there a buyer? Who will buy the product: an abattoir, a fresh produce market, a packhouse, a retailer, a silo, local people?
  • Distance to the market and the condition of roads. Fresh vegetables and milk spoil quickly and need to be near buyers. Grain and wool can travel further.
  • Price and demand – are prices stable, and is demand growing or falling?
  • Quality standards – some buyers require certification or strict grading.

Economic factors

  • Capital – how much money is needed to start, for example to plant an orchard, build a dairy, or buy cattle?
  • Time to income – vegetables can bring income within months; fruit and nut trees may take several years before the first good harvest.
  • Running costs – feed, fertiliser, fuel, labour.
  • Expected profit – gross margin per hectare or per animal compared with other options.
  • Risk – how much could be lost in a bad year?

Resources on the farm

  • Labour: is enough skilled labour available? Dairies and vegetables need many hours; extensive cattle need fewer.
  • Equipment and buildings already on the farm.
  • Infrastructure: electricity, roads, fences, handling facilities, cold rooms.

Personal factors

  • The farmer's knowledge, skills and experience.
  • Personal interest and lifestyle: a dairy needs work every day, including weekends.
  • Family goals and culture, for example the value of cattle.

Government and support

Laws, support schemes, extension advice and access to finance can encourage or limit some enterprises.

Putting it together

A farmer lists possible enterprises, checks each against all these factors, and rejects those that do not fit. The best enterprise matches the natural resources, has a reliable market, fits the money and skills available, and carries risk the farmer can manage.

Key points

  • An enterprise is one farming activity producing a product.
  • Climate, soil, water, terrain and diseases set natural limits.
  • A reliable market and access to it are essential.
  • Capital, time to income, costs, profit and risk must be considered.
  • Labour, equipment, skills and personal goals also shape the choice.

The Karoo with very low rainfall
